name: Felix Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy beer, wine, cider and soft drinks for Marlow and Dunn, a drinks distributor that supplies pubs, hotels and restaurants. Mornings I use an AI tool to predict what the pubs will need, using fixtures, weather and local events. A big match or a warm weekend can double our orders for lager. Then I'm on the phone with the brewers and the wine importers, and I finish with a stock check in the cold store.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the mix of numbers and pubs. I can walk into a landlord's bar, listen to what's selling, and go back to the screen and make it work. What wears me out is the swings: a wet summer, a pub closing, a duty change and my forecast is wrong. At home, my wife Claire is a teaching assistant, and we've got Tom, eleven, and Ruby, eight. I coach Tom's football team on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools I've got are doing fine. At work I'd tell the lads it's a decent assistant if you give it good information. At the football club I'd say the hype was loud and the change was small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm okay with that, but it would take the shine off. I've got a head start because I use AI daily and the rest of the team doesn't, and it gives me a bit of standing. If it doesn't go further, that gap closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what I use and polish it. I'd improve my forecast model, and train one of the juniors on it, so I'm the one who's made the team better. And I'd ask for a pay review, because it's my model and it's saved us stock write-offs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit bored. It feels like the third quarter of a match where nothing happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would a flat, hype-free version change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. Claire's wage and mine barely cover the mortgage and the kids. We've less than a month of savings, and pubs closing means my customers vanish. There aren't many other distributors round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the pressure on you and Claire in the background?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet summer. If a wet summer hits the pubs, they cut orders, my bonus goes, and we feel it. That's what I think about, not AI.

say: I'd tell the lads it's a decent assistant if you give it **good information**.
At football I'd say the hype was loud and the change small.
think: If AI doesn't go further, the **gap** between me and colleagues closes and I lose some standing.
A bad summer for pubs would cut my bonus.
do: Polish my **forecast model** and train one junior to use it.
Ask for a **pay review** because the model has saved stock write-offs.
feel: **Fine**, a bit bored; it feels like the third quarter of a match where nothing happens.
S0.quote: If a wet summer hits the pubs, they cut orders, my bonus goes, and we feel it. That's what I think about, not AI.
fieldNote: Felix's unease is about **money and pubs closing**, not about technology.
He sees AI skill as personal standing and wants a pay review for it.
He is cheerful and practical, using sports talk to cope.

steps.text: Improve the pub-demand forecast model using fixtures and weather
Train one junior buyer to use the model
Ask for a pay review citing stock write-offs saved
Move the bonus straight into savings each quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's be the team that runs the pilots, and I'll lead. At the football club I'd say this is why kids need a skill and a bit of grit. Online I'd say it needs common sense and not too many rules from the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm one of the safer ones, because I already do half of what the new tools do. But the team of six becomes three or four, and I'd feel I'd got lucky to keep my job, not that I deserved it. That doesn't sit right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take over the forecasting for the whole range, and automate the reorders for the pubs we've served for years. I'd ask for a lead role and a pay rise. I'd also start a side job: pub quiz nights and tasting evenings, because it's something I enjoy and it earns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keen and uncomfortable. I like the work and I like winning, but I know it costs others their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is named on the card. How do you see your own role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two juniors who do the order entry and the invoice checking. They're good lads, but they're the first to go. I'd teach them everything I know, and maybe help them find work in sales, where a person still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd save every extra pound. Being ahead of the pack is no use if the firm shrinks and I'm the only one carrying the bills.

say: I'd say let's be the team that runs the **pilots**, and I'll lead.
Online I'd say it needs common sense and not too many **rules**.
think: I'm one of the safer ones because I already do half of what the new tools do.
A team of six becomes **three or four**, and I'd feel lucky, not deserving.
do: Take over **forecasting** for the whole range and automate reorders for long-term pubs.
Ask for a **lead role** and a pay rise.
Start a side job running pub quiz and tasting evenings.
feel: **Keen** and uncomfortable; I like winning but I know it costs others their jobs.
S1.quote: I'd feel I'd got lucky to keep my job, not that I deserved it. That doesn't sit right.
fieldNote: Felix expects to be among the **survivors** and feels guilty about it.
He plans to teach the juniors and point them towards sales.
A pub-quiz side job fits his sociable traditional outlook.

steps.text: Automate the reorders for long-standing pub customers
Run pub quiz and beer-tasting nights on weekends
Save every extra pound from the pay rise
Teach the two juniors the forecasting tools before any cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a clear plan and we need it now. At the football club I'd say let's look after each other, because there'll be dads out of work. I'd probably say nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm out of a job, and so is nearly everyone like me. Even with the tools I'm good at, the machine will be better than me and cheaper. I'd say my job has two years, three at the outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd move into whatever is hands-on in the firm: the cold store, the delivery side, the pub relationships. Robots come about three years after the AI, so that gives me until 2031. I'd also start the tasting-night business properly, and I'd offer to run drinks for local weddings. We'd cut everything extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rattled. I don't scare easily, but I'd be up at four in the morning doing sums. It's the mortgage and the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What does your own job look like then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit her down and tell her what I think and what I'll do. I'd say, I've got a plan, and it'll be hard, but we'll manage. She'd say, you've never been afraid of work, and that would hold me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do first, and what do you say to Claire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other thing is the football club. A lot of people there work hands-on, and they'd have a few more years. I'd lean on that network for any odd jobs.

say: I'd say we need a clear **plan** and we need it now.
At the football club I'd say we should look after each other.
think: I'm out of a job, since the machine will be better and **cheaper**, and my job has two years, maybe three.
The football club network might give odd jobs for a few more years.
do: Move towards **hands-on** work in the firm: cold store, delivery and pub relationships.
Start the **tasting-night** business properly and offer drinks for weddings.
feel: **Rattled**; I'd be up at four in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: I don't scare easily, but I'd be up at four in the morning doing sums.
fieldNote: Felix expects to **lose** his job in two to three years and moves quickly to hands-on work.
His adaptability shows in the plan, but not in his sleep.
He leans on Claire and the football club.

steps.text: Move into cold-store, delivery or pub-relationship work at the firm
Launch tasting nights and wedding drinks as a proper business
Cut every extra spend at home from week one
Lean on football club families for odd jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway and we should use it well. At work I'd say let's plan the changes properly. At the club I'd say apprenticeships are the way for kids who like working with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the desk part of my job goes by 2031, but I'd have time to move. I'm the type who goes early, so I'd probably be fine, but there's no guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by building the side business to a point where it covers a third of our bills. I'd get a licence for running events, and take a short course in logistics. I'd save four hundred a month, so after two years we'd have a proper cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd say fired up. It's like a cup final, where you've got to turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What can you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that whatever happens, they should learn to work with people. Machines will do spreadsheets, but they can't run a pub night or put an arm round a mate. That, and learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tom's team, if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The best part of five years is the ability to try things. If the side business doesn't work, I've got time to try another.

say: I'd say five years is a decent **runway** and we should plan properly.
At the club I'd say **apprenticeships** suit kids who like working with their hands.
think: The desk part of my job goes by **2031**, but I'd have time to move.
I go early, so I'd probably be fine, but there's no guarantee.
do: Build the side business until it covers a **third** of our bills.
Get an events licence and take a short **logistics** course.
feel: **Anxious** but fired up, like turning up for a cup final.
S3.quote: Machines will do spreadsheets, but they can't run a pub night or put an arm round a mate.
fieldNote: Felix **tests** a side business, treating five years as a chance to try things.
He links human skills to his sociable, community life.
Mood is anxious because his desk job still goes within the window.

steps.text: Grow the tasting-night business until it covers a third of the bills
Take a logistics course and get an events licence
Save four hundred a month for two years
Bring Tom along to help at the events, so he sees the work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and we shouldn't waste it worrying. At work I'd say keep building. At the football club I'd say get the kids learning real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be okay. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be at university, and I'd have my own little business going. I'd just need the next few years to be steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep improving what I do with AI, and put money aside for the kids' university. I'd build the events business slowly and perhaps buy a small van for it in year three. I'd pay the mortgage down a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. Ten years takes the sting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. How does your plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the mortgage nearly gone and Tom and Ruby on their feet. Most of all I want to be doing work I'd choose, not work I was pushed into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be true by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it works out, I'll have a business that doesn't need me to be at a desk. That's a nice thought.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty and we shouldn't waste it **worrying**.
At the club I'd say get the kids learning real skills.
think: By 2036 I'd be fifty-three with the kids at **university** and my own small business going.
I need the next few years to be steady.
do: Keep improving what I do with **AI** and put aside money for university.
Build the events business slowly and buy a small **van** in year three.
Pay the mortgage down a bit faster.

S4.quote: Most of all I want to be doing work I'd choose, not work I was pushed into.
fieldNote: Ten years makes Felix **relaxed**, with the side business as his path.
The near years are still tight, so his unease stays.
He values choosing his own work over being pushed.

steps.text: Keep improving the forecasting model as the AI tools get better
Save for Tom's and Ruby's university costs
Buy a small van for the events business in year three
Build the events business slowly at weekends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. We'd have no cushion and I'd have no time to get the business going. What would help is the firm telling us early, a government that doesn't over-regulate but does back apprenticeships and small business loans, and my football club mates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that using AI every day doesn't mean I'm relaxed. I'm good with these tools, but I've a mortgage, two kids and almost no savings. A good player can still lose the match.

headlineQuote: Using AI every day doesn't mean I'm relaxed. I'm good with these tools, but I've a mortgage, two kids and almost no savings.
portrait: Felix Walsh, 43, is a senior **buyer** for a pub-and-hotel drinks distributor, with a teaching-assistant wife, two kids and a mortgage.
He's traditional, community-minded and **adaptive**: he uses AI daily and built his own pub-demand forecasting model.
Thin savings and pubs' ups and downs keep him uneasy even when AI plateaus.
In faster scenarios he expects the desk job to go and moves into **hands-on** work and a tasting-night business.
He leans on Claire and his football club, and blames red tape more than technology.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, with no cushion and no time to get his own business going.
whatWouldHelp: Early **notice** from the firm, apprenticeships and small business loans, and his football club mates.
